content: Reduced cardiorespiratory fitness, also known as cardiorespiratory deconditioning, is a frequent consequence of traumatic brain injury (TBI). Fitness training programs may be utilized to address this specific impairment. The primary aim of this updated review was to assess whether fitness training improves cardiorespiratory fitness in individuals who have experienced a TBI. Secondary objectives included evaluating whether fitness training has an impact on physical and cognitive impairments, psychological outcomes, activity limitations, and participation restrictions. Additionally, the review sought to determine the safety, acceptance, feasibility, and overall suitability of fitness training for this population. To gather relevant data, the researchers conducted a comprehensive search across 10 electronic databases, including the Cochrane Injuries Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, Embase, PubMed (MEDLINE), CINAHL, AMED, SPORTDiscus, PsycINFO, PEDro, and PsycBITE. They also searched the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform and reviewed reference lists from related systematic reviews and included studies. Trialists were contacted to identify additional studies. The search was last conducted in August 2017. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving participants with TBI. Eligible studies compared an exercise program incorporating cardiorespiratory fitness training to usual care, a non-exercise intervention, or no intervention. Two independent authors screened the search results, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Additional information was requested from trialists when necessary. For continuous data, mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. For dichotomous data, odds ratios with 95% CI were used. Data were pooled when sufficient homogeneity was present across studies. This updated review identified two new studies with 96 participants, which were added to six previously included studies, resulting in a total of eight studies with 399 participants. The majority of participants were men in their mid-thirties who had sustained severe TBI. None of the studies included children. The studies varied significantly in terms of interventions, time since injury, and outcome measures. At the end of the intervention, the mean difference in peak power output was 35.47 watts (W) in favor of fitness training (MD 35.47 W, 95% CI 2.53 to 68.41 W; 3 studies, 67 participants; low-quality evidence). However, the confidence intervals included both a potentially clinically significant effect and a negligible effect, and there was moderate heterogeneity among the studies. Five secondary outcomes had sufficient data for meta-analysis at the end of the intervention. These included: Body composition: The standardized mean difference (SMD) was 0.29 standard deviations favoring the control group (95% CI -0.22 to 0.79; 2 studies, 61 participants; low-quality evidence). Strength: The SMD was -0.02 favoring the control group (95% CI -0.86 to 0.83; 2 studies, 23 participants; very low-quality evidence). Fatigue: The SMD was -0.32 favoring fitness training (95% CI -0.90 to 0.26; 3 studies, 130 participants; very low-quality evidence). Depression: The SMD was -0.43 favoring fitness training (95% CI -0.92 to 0.06; 4 studies, 220 participants; very low-quality evidence). Neuromotor function: The mean difference was 0.01 meters favoring fitness training (95% CI -0.25 to 0.27; 2 studies, 109 participants; moderate-quality evidence). The evidence was inconclusive regarding whether fitness training was more or less effective than control interventions for these secondary outcomes. Quality of life was assessed in three trials, but the data were not pooled due to substantial heterogeneity. No adverse events were reported in any of the included studies, and five of the eight studies reported no dropouts from their intervention groups. This suggests that fitness training was generally well-tolerated by participants with TBI. The authors concluded that there is low-quality evidence supporting the effectiveness of fitness training in improving cardiorespiratory fitness after TBI. However, there is insufficient evidence to draw definitive conclusions about its effects on other outcomes. While fitness training appears to be safe and accepted by individuals with TBI, further well-designed and adequately powered studies are needed to provide more precise estimates of its effects on cardiorespiratory fitness and other important outcomes. Future research should also explore the impact of fitness training on diverse populations, including children. In the absence of high-quality evidence, clinicians are advised to use pre-exercise screening checklists to ensure the safety of individuals with TBI before initiating exercise programs. Training parameters should be guided by the American College of Sports Medicine's recommendations for individuals with brain injuries.
